title: the man who argued with God about Sodom
hookLine: the man who argued with God about Sodom
last: ARGUE TO LEARN, NOT TO WIN.

lines: A TENT IN THE HEAT OF THE DAY.
cards: An old man is sitting at the door of his tent in the heat of the day. Three visitors arrive, he feeds them, and as they leave, God tells him something.
The cities of the plain, Sodom and Gomorrah, have done terrible things, and God is going to see about them. He could bow, or nod, or quietly go back inside. He doesn't.
The text says he comes closer. And then he starts to argue. With God.
Today: an argument with God, and the man who made it.

teach.b: Abraham. Born Abram, the text says, and renamed when God promised he'd be the father of many nations. Jews call him Avraham avinu, Abraham our father.
What if there are fifty good people in the city? Will you sweep them away with the rest? Then comes the line at the center of the story: "Shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?"
That takes nerve. He's holding God to God's own standard.
And God answers: for fifty, I'll spare it. So Abraham keeps going. Forty-five?
Each time he gets more polite, and more stubborn. He calls himself "but dust and ashes," and still doesn't back down. He stops at ten.
Why ten? The text doesn't say. Some teachers note that ten is the smallest number that makes a community.
In the end, ten good people aren't found. But the argument is never scolded. God listens to every round.
And Abraham isn't the last. Moses argues with God later. So does Job.
The psalms complain out loud. There's a Hasidic story of a rabbi who put God on trial on behalf of his people.
Arguing with God, in this tradition, isn't the opposite of faith.

teach.h: SHALL NOT THE JUDGE OF ALL THE EARTH DO JUSTLY?
teach.b: It's one of the ways faith talks.

how: Jews read Abraham's argument over Sodom in the Torah portion Vayera each autumn, and the Jewish tradition of questioning and arguing, with God and with one another, runs through the Psalms, Job and the Talmud's recorded debates.

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: his name before God renamed him

s: God answers every round. the argument is never scolded.
Abraham bargains down from fifty to ten
fifty, forty-five, forty, thirty, twenty, ten.

games.q: you're Abraham. God has just told you Sodom will be judged. what do you do?
o: bow and go back into the tent.
come closer and argue for the innocent.
games.why: he comes closer: "shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly?" and bargains from fifty down to ten.

practice: Forty-five seconds, with the bell. Bring to mind one thing that seems unfair to you right now, in your life or in the world. Don't smooth it over.
Say it plainly, inside. If you pray, you can say it to God the way Abraham did: direct, respectful, and not backing down. If you don't, say it honestly to yourself.

wordCard.voice: Abraham. Father of many nations, who argued with God on behalf of strangers. Eighth word.

orig.note: Hebrew: the text links the new name to av hamon goyim, father of many nations.

carryVoice: Your line: you're allowed to argue. Direct, respectful, and on behalf of someone else: that's how Abraham did it. Day eight.
